title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Safe Medication Practice
intro:
Welcome to GNPS Program 3 - Safe Medication Practice. Medication administration is one of the most frequent and high-risk responsibilities performed by nurses. Every tablet, injection, infusion or topical medicine requires careful assessment, accurate preparation, correct identification and ongoing observation. Safe medication practice begins with understanding how medicines work and following reliable checks every time. This level is designed around the pharmacology and medication-management capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies in different countries. It develops the essential knowledge, calculation skills, professional attitudes and practical behaviours required to administer medicines safely within the nurse's scope of practice. What You Will Learn Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Explain basic pharmacological principles and common medication classifications Understand how medicines are absorbed, distributed, metabolised and eliminated Apply the Rights of Medication Administration consistently Calculate common medication doses accurately Prepare and administer medicines through common routes Recognise allergies, contraindications, interactions and adverse reactions Monitor and evaluate the patient's response to medicines Document medication administration accurately Educate patients about safe and effective medication use Why This Learning Matters A medication error can occur at any stage: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering or monitoring. Nurses provide the final safety check before many medicines reach the patient. Careful assessment, correct calculation and consistent verification can prevent serious harm. Remember...
Safe medication practice depends on knowledge, attention and accountability. Your Learning Goal By the end of Level 1, you should be able to calculate, prepare, administer, monitor and document commonly used medicines safely while following national standards, organisational procedures and your scope of practice.

sections.title: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety

content.text: Pharmacology is the study of medicines and their effects on the body. Nurses do not need to memorise every medicine, but they must understand the principles that explain why a medicine is given, how it works, what effects are expected and what risks require monitoring. Safe medication practice begins before the medicine is prepared.
Learning outcomes
Explain basic pharmacological terminology Describe how medicines move through the body
Identify common medication classifications Relate pharmacological knowledge to safe nursing care

Medication Names and Classifications A medicine may have a generic name and one or more brand names. The generic name is usually preferred in professional communication because brand names differ between countries and manufacturers. Medicines are grouped into classes according to their action or purpose, such as antibiotics, analgesics, antihypertensives, anticoagulants and diuretics.

Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a medicine. It includes absorption into the circulation, distribution to tissues, metabolism - commonly in the liver - and elimination, often through the kidneys. Age, hydration, organ function and route of administration can alter these processes.

Pharmacodynamics describes what the medicine does to the body. Medicines may stimulate, block or modify physiological processes. Understanding the intended action helps the nurse recognise whether the treatment is effective and identify unwanted effects.

Therapeutic and Unwanted Effects The therapeutic effect is the intended benefit. Side effects are predictable secondary effects, while adverse reactions may be harmful or unexpected. Toxicity can occur when a medicine accumulates or is given in excessive amounts. Nurses should know the main therapeutic purpose and important risks of every medicine they administer.

A patient with heart failure is prescribed a diuretic. Before administration, the nurse checks the patient's blood pressure, fluid balance and recent electrolyte results. The nurse understands that the medicine should reduce excess fluid but may also contribute to dehydration, low blood pressure or electrolyte imbalance. Pharmacological knowledge guides both administration and monitoring.
Key learning points
Know why each medicine is prescribed Use generic names whenever possible
Consider liver and kidney function when medicines are cleared from the body
Monitor both therapeutic effects and unwanted effects

sections.title: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely

content.text: Medication administration combines calculation, practical skill and professional judgement. A correct order can still cause harm if the dose is calculated incorrectly, the wrong route is used or the medicine is given without identifying the patient. Reliable safety checks should be followed even during busy periods.
Learning outcomes
Apply the Rights of Medication Administration Perform basic medication calculations accurately
Prepare medicines using safe and aseptic practice Administer medicines through common routes

Rights of Medication Administration The recognised rights commonly include the right patient, medicine, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, assessment, education, evaluation and the patient's right to refuse. Organisations may use different lists, but the purpose is the same: to create deliberate checks before, during and after administration.

Medication Calculations Dose calculations should be completed using an approved method and checked for reasonableness. The basic relationship is often expressed as required dose divided by available dose, multiplied by the available quantity. Decimal points, unit conversion and paediatric or weight-based doses require particular care.

Preparation The medication order, label, expiry date, concentration and integrity of the product should be checked. Medicines should be prepared for one patient at a time in a clean area with minimal interruption. Unlabelled or unclear products must not be used.

Routes of Administration Common routes include oral, sublingual, topical, inhaled, enteral, subcutaneous, intramuscular and intravenous. Each route has specific requirements. The nurse must confirm competence, assess whether the route is appropriate and observe the patient after administration.

A prescription requires 500 mg of an antibiotic. The vial contains 250 mg in 5 mL. The nurse calculates that 10 mL is required, checks the calculation against the order, confirms the patient's identity and allergy status, and asks for a second check when required by policy. The medicine is then administered and documented promptly.
Key learning points
Use the medication rights every time Check calculations and units carefully
Prepare medicines for one patient at a time Never administer an unclear, damaged or unlabelled product

sections.title: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions

content.text: Medication safety continues after a medicine is given. Nurses must observe for benefit, side effects, allergy, interaction and deterioration. Early recognition and prompt action can prevent a mild reaction from becoming a serious emergency.
Learning outcomes
Identify common causes of medication errors Recognise adverse drug reactions and allergy
Understand basic contraindications and interactions Respond appropriately to medication incidents

Medication Errors Errors may involve the wrong patient, medicine, dose, route or time, omitted doses, duplicate therapy or incomplete documentation. Contributing factors include interruptions, look-alike packaging, unclear orders, fatigue and failure to follow identification processes.

Allergy and Adverse Drug Reactions An allergy involves an immune response and may present as rash, swelling, wheeze or anaphylaxis. Other adverse reactions may include bleeding, severe nausea, confusion, low blood pressure or organ toxicity. The nurse should distinguish a known side effect from a potentially serious reaction.

Contraindications and Interactions A contraindication is a reason a medicine may be unsuitable, such as pregnancy, severe kidney impairment or a previous serious allergy. Interactions can occur between medicines, food, alcohol or herbal products. Reviewing the complete medication history is essential.

Responding to an Incident If an error or serious reaction occurs, immediate patient assessment and treatment take priority. The nurse should seek assistance, notify the appropriate clinician, document the clinical event and complete incident reporting according to policy. Concealing an error increases risk.

Shortly after receiving an intravenous antibiotic, a patient develops itching, facial swelling and difficulty breathing. The nurse stops the infusion, calls for emergency assistance, maintains the airway, follows the emergency medication protocol and documents the event. The allergy information is updated clearly to prevent re-exposure.
Key learning points
Assess the patient before and after medication administration Treat new breathing difficulty or swelling as an emergency
Review medicines, food and supplements for possible interactions Report errors and near misses so that future harm can be prevented

Safe medication practice is both a clinical and professional responsibility. Nurses must practise within their authority, document accurately and ensure that patients understand how to use medicines safely. Medication education is not an optional extra; it is part of effective treatment.
Learning outcomes
Explain professional accountability in medication administration Document medication care accurately and promptly
Respect the patient's right to information and refusal Provide clear medication education

Professional Accountability The nurse is accountable for assessing the patient, checking the order, preparing and administering safely, monitoring the response and seeking clarification when needed. A prescriber's order does not remove the nurse's responsibility to question an unsafe or unclear instruction.

Documentation Medication records should show what was administered, when, by which route and by whom. Omitted, delayed or refused doses should be recorded with the reason and relevant follow-up. Documentation should never be completed before the medicine is actually given.

Consent and Refusal Patients have the right to understand the purpose, expected benefit and important risks of treatment. A competent patient may refuse a medicine. The nurse should explore concerns, provide information, notify the appropriate clinician and document the refusal without coercion.

Patient Education Education should include the medicine's name, purpose, dose, timing, method of use, important side effects, interactions, storage and when to seek help. Plain language, written information and teach-back improve understanding and adherence.

Mrs Patel is prescribed a new anticoagulant. The nurse explains why it is needed, how and when to take it, the importance of not doubling missed doses and the signs of bleeding that require urgent review. Mrs Patel is then asked to explain the instructions in her own words. A misunderstanding is corrected before discharge.
Key learning points
Question any order that appears unsafe or unclear Document only after administration
Respect informed refusal Use teach-back to confirm understanding

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 3 - Level 1, you have developed the essential knowledge and practical skills required to understand basic pharmacology, calculate and administer medicines safely, recognise adverse reactions and educate patients. These capabilities provide the foundation for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where medication decisions become more complex and are applied within international systems and multidisciplinary care.
